questions.prompt: Your uncle sits with his son the whole evening before a difficult journey and keeps telling him that he will be fine and that the family is behind him. Which of the four family roles is he playing?

options.text: Provision of resources
Life skills development
Nurturance and support
Maintenance and management of the family system

questions.explanation: "Nurturance and support" is the affective role, the one that gives comfort, warmth and reassurance, and an evening of encouragement gives exactly that. "Provision of resources" covers money, food, clothing and shelter, and nothing material changes hands here. "Life skills development" would mean teaching his son something he does not yet know how to do, and the uncle teaches nothing. "Maintenance and management of the family system" covers decisions, finances, discipline and standards, none of which appears in the scene.

questions.prompt: Which sentence describes an automatic result — what happens every single time, not on one particular day?

options.text: If you raise your voice, my little brother stops talking.
If you raise your voice tomorrow evening, my little brother will stop talking.
If you raised your voice, my little brother would stop talking.
If you had raised your voice, my little brother would have stopped talking.

questions.explanation: An automatic or habitual result keeps a present tense in both halves, so the sentence is "If you raise your voice, my little brother stops talking.": every time the first thing happens, the second follows. "If you raise your voice tomorrow evening, my little brother will stop talking." uses will and names an evening, so it predicts one single occasion instead of stating a rule. "If you raised your voice, my little brother would stop talking." imagines something that is not happening. "If you had raised your voice, my little brother would have stopped talking." looks back at something that never happened at all.

questions.prompt: Complete: "My parents never let me ___ the house before the washing up is done."

options.text: to leave
leaving
leaves
leave

questions.explanation: After let plus its object the verb keeps its base form, which gives let me "leave". "to leave" adds the to that belongs to want, never to let. "leaving" would need an auxiliary such as am or was in front of it. "leaves" puts back the present -s of he, she and it on a verb that let has already stripped bare.

questions.prompt: Your father has one wish for you: you should choose engineering. Which sentence says it in English?

options.text: My father wants that I choose engineering.
My father wants me to choose engineering.
My father wants me choosing engineering.
My father wants me choose engineering.

questions.explanation: English states the wish with want plus the person plus to plus the base verb: "My father wants me to choose engineering." "My father wants that I choose engineering." copies the subordinate clause of French and Arabic, and want never takes one in English. "My father wants me choose engineering." drops the to that this structure always needs, and "My father wants me choosing engineering." puts an -ing form where only a to-infinitive can stand.

questions.prompt: Nadia says: "If my father comes home late, he eats alone in the kitchen." What does her sentence tell you?

options.text: Her father is coming home late this particular evening.
Whenever he is late, that is what happens.
Her father will probably be late again tomorrow evening.
Her father came home late once and ate on his own.

questions.explanation: Two present tenses on either side of if describe a result that follows automatically every time the condition is met, so the sentence means that whenever he is late, that is what happens. "Her father is coming home late this particular evening" turns a habit into one single evening, which is what a present continuous would say, not this pattern. "Her father will probably be late again tomorrow evening" reads the sentence as a prediction, but there is no will anywhere in it, and this structure never predicts. "Her father came home late once and ate on his own" puts the whole thing in the past, while both verbs here are in the present.
